name: Montana

notes: Groceries aren't taxed; resort taxes don't apply to food bought unprepared.
Full-service restaurants and quick-service restaurants: restaurant food and drinks pay no state tax; resort communities and areas add 3% or 4%, counted where they apply year-round.

Liquor is sold through state agency stores at prices that include the state's 40.5% markup and excise and license taxes of up to 16% and 10% of the retail price (by the distiller's size); beer pays $1.30 to $4.30 a barrel and table wine 27 cents a liter. Left out here; drinks served in resort communities' bars and restaurants pay the resort tax, counted in the restaurant rate.

Cigarettes pay $1.70 a pack of 20, other tobacco 50% of the wholesale price, moist snuff 85 cents an ounce and premium cigars 50% of the wholesale price or 35 cents each, whichever is less; left out here.

Household supplies, pets and toys, personal care products, clothing, home furnishings, and auto parts: Montana has no sales tax on goods; in resort communities, luxuries sold to visitors pay the resort tax, which isn't counted here.
Barber and beauty services, laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: Montana doesn't tax these services.
Gasoline pays 33 cents a gallon and diesel 29.75 cents, left out here.

Montana has no general sales tax. Resort taxes of 3% or 4% apply year-round in Big Sky, Red Lodge, Whitefish, Columbia Falls, West Yellowstone, the Cooke City area (with Silver Gate) and St. Regis, and for part of the year in Virginia City, Craig, Gardiner and Wolf Creek; since 2025 voters may also spend the extra 1% on workforce housing (SB 172, HB 162).

Lodging pays the state's 8% (a 4% lodging facility use tax and a 4% sales tax) plus any resort tax, and car rentals 4%; adult-use marijuana pays 20% and medical marijuana 4% (MCA 15-64-102). Not counted here.
A 2025 bill to let local governments levy a tourism tax of up to 4% (HB 489) died in the legislature (as reported).
gaps: Montana has no state or local general sales tax.

Resort communities and resort areas levy a resort tax of up to 3%, plus up to 1% more for infrastructure or housing where voters approve it (MCA 7-6-1503), on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries. It is counted in the restaurant categories wherever it applies year-round: in the figures where the community or area holds at least half a census tract (Big Sky 4%, Red Lodge 4%, Whitefish 3%, Columbia Falls 3%), and named on the pages of West Yellowstone (4%), Cooke City and Silver Gate (3%) and St. Regis (3%), each under half of its tract. Seasonal taxes (Virginia City, Craig, Gardiner, Wolf Creek) and the Big Mountain and Red Lodge Mountain resort areas, which aren't Census places, are named on the pages they touch, not counted. Which goods count as luxuries is set locally, so the tax is not applied to the other categories.

Unincorporated resort areas (Big Sky, Cooke City, Craig, Gardiner, St. Regis, Wolf Creek) are recorded on the Census place of the same name (Cooke City's also on Silver Gate), whose boundary may differ from the resort area's.
Lodging pays the state's 8% (a 4% lodging facility use tax and a 4% sales tax) and car rentals 4% (MCA 15-65-111, 15-68-102); not counted here.

3006325: Big Sky's resort tax is 4% (3% plus 1% for infrastructure since July 1, 2020) on lodging, restaurants and bars, ski areas and other destination recreation, and luxuries in the Big Sky Resort Area District, which spans Gallatin and Madison counties and runs to 2032; it is counted in Big Sky's restaurant rate (Big Sky Resort Area District).
3016600: Columbia Falls' 3% resort tax on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries, running through September 30, 2040 (city code chapter 3.20, adopted with Ordinance 80 in October 2020 after the June 2, 2020 election), is counted in Columbia Falls' restaurant rate.
3017350: The Cooke City resort area, which also takes in Silver Gate, levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it is counted in Cooke City's restaurant rate.
3018025: The Craig resort area levies a 4% resort tax from April 1 to November 15 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce; the Department of Revenue's list gives 3%); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3029950: The Gardiner resort area levies a 4% resort tax from June 1 to September 30 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3061525: Red Lodge's resort tax is 4% (3% renewed by voters on June 2, 2020, plus 1% for stormwater projects since July 7, 2020) on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries; it is counted in Red Lodge's restaurant rate (City of Red Lodge; the Department of Commerce's map still shows 3%).
The Red Lodge Mountain resort area, the ski area west of the city, has levied a 2% resort tax since January 1, 2008 (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since the area isn't a Census place.
3065575: The St. Regis resort area levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it is counted in St. Regis' restaurant rate.
3068425: Silver Gate is in the Cooke City resort area, which levies a 3% resort tax year-round on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); it is counted in Silver Gate's restaurant rate.
3077125: Virginia City levies a 4% resort tax from April through October on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
3079525: West Yellowstone's resort tax is 4% on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (3% since 1986 and 1% more for infrastructure, approved in 2019; Town of West Yellowstone); it is counted in West Yellowstone's restaurant rate.
3079825: Whitefish's 3% resort tax on lodging, restaurant and prepared food, alcoholic drinks, ski resort goods and services and luxuries (approved in 1995 and extended by voters in 2021 to January 31, 2045) is counted in Whitefish's restaurant rate (City of Whitefish).

The Big Mountain Resort Area District around Whitefish Mountain Resort, outside the city, levies a 3% resort tax from June 1, 2025, for 20 years (approved 80 to 10 in Flathead County's special election of January 21, 2025, per the county's certified canvass; the Department of Commerce's map still shows its rate as yet to be set); not counted here, since the district isn't a Census place.
3081400: The Wolf Creek resort area levies a 3% resort tax from April 1 to November 15 on lodging, restaurants and bars, destination recreation and luxuries (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since it applies only part of the year.
30009: The Red Lodge Mountain resort area, the ski area west of the city, has levied a 2% resort tax since January 1, 2008 (Department of Commerce); not counted here, since the area isn't a Census place.
30029: The Big Mountain Resort Area District around Whitefish Mountain Resort, outside the city, levies a 3% resort tax from June 1, 2025, for 20 years (approved 80 to 10 in Flathead County's special election of January 21, 2025, per the county's certified canvass; the Department of Commerce's map still shows its rate as yet to be set); not counted here, since the district isn't a Census place.

3017350: Cooke City holds less than half of the residents of each census tract it is in. Its own page uses its own rates; a selection of whole census tracts, like this one, counts its restaurant tax for the 8% of the tract's jobs at restaurants, bars and hotels located in Cooke City, and the surrounding area's rates for the rest of the tract, since sales tax is charged where purchases are made (LEHD LODES 2024 jobs by census block).
3065575: St. Regis holds less than half of the residents of each census tract it is in. Its own page uses its own rates; a selection of whole census tracts, like this one, counts its restaurant tax for the 22% of the tract's jobs at restaurants, bars and hotels located in St. Regis, and the surrounding area's rates for the rest of the tract, since sales tax is charged where purchases are made (LEHD LODES 2024 jobs by census block).
3068425: Silver Gate holds less than half of the residents of each census tract it is in. Its own page uses its own rates; a selection of whole census tracts, like this one, counts its restaurant tax for the 2% of the tract's jobs at restaurants, bars and hotels located in Silver Gate, and the surrounding area's rates for the rest of the tract, since sales tax is charged where purchases are made (LEHD LODES 2024 jobs by census block).

programs: Tax increment financing districts (urban renewal, targeted economic development, industrial and technology districts) are mapped statewide from the Department of Revenue's layer (updated November 2025), each named with its city or county; three it still lists as existing ended July 1, 2026 (Missoula's Technology District and Kalispell's Old School Technology G and Industrial H districts) and are left out. Business improvement districts are mapped from city and county layers in Great Falls, Livingston, Missoula, Helena, Kalispell and Bozeman (the city's base layer), and Billings' downtown district from the Department of Commerce's map (November 2026), which follows the Downtown Billings Partnership's map; Commerce notes that the 2010 expansion's legal description and map don't match and that it is still confirming the exact boundary. Communities in the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program are named on their pages.

warn.text: Bozeman draws many visitors (Montana State University, Bridger Bowl and travelers bound for Big Sky and Yellowstone National Park), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Bozeman is an affiliate community of the Department of Commerce's Main Street Montana Program; its downtown isn't mapped.
Downtown Bozeman's business improvement district isn't mapped: the city publishes no layer of it.

warn.text: Helena Valley Northeast's visitor caution draws on the census tract it shares with Craig, Wolf Creek and York along the Missouri River, whose cabins and fishing lodging (584 of its 1,970 homes seasonal, 29.6%; 10 lodging places) lie mostly outside Helena Valley Northeast, though about half of the tract's residents live in it, so read that caution with care.

Pryor's page is built from the census tract it shares with Fort Smith and St. Xavier, whose fishing lodges on the Bighorn River and cabins by Bighorn Canyon (132 of 593 homes seasonal, 22.3%; 12 lodging places) give the tract its visitor caution more than Pryor itself, so read that caution with care.

St. Xavier's page is built from the census tract it shares with Fort Smith and Pryor, whose fishing lodges on the Bighorn River and cabins by Bighorn Canyon (132 of 593 homes seasonal, 22.3%; 12 lodging places) give the tract its visitor caution more than St. Xavier itself, so read that caution with care.

Glendive's visitor caution draws on the lodging in its census tract (16 lodging places, 3.6 per 1,000 residents, with few seasonal homes, 2.6%), likely serving travelers on Interstate 94 and oil-field and rail workers more than tourists, so read that caution with care.
